result: Macrophages release ~30-nm cholesterol-rich particles that are fragments of the plasma membrane pulled away and left behind during the projection and retraction of filopodia and lamellipodia. Correlative live-cell microscopy and SEM showed particles deposited where filopodia/lamellipodia had extended and retracted.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C17, and C62 are well-supported by correlative live-cell microscopy and SEM imaging (Figure 1) showing spatial and temporal correspondence between filopodia/lamellipodia movement and particle deposition. The biotinylation experiments (C26-C28, C62) provide additional evidence that particles contain plasma membrane components.

result: Blocking cell movement with latrunculin A or blebbistatin abolishes particle release from macrophages. Pre-treatment with either drug prevented particle release, while post-adherence treatment with latrunculin A left a circumferential ring of particles as cells retracted. Particle release resumed after drug removal.
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C18-C23 are supported by SEM images (Figure 2) and live-cell imaging showing that inhibiting actin polymerization or myosin II activity blocks particle release. The reversibility experiment (C23) and the post-adherence latrunculin A experiment (C20) provide strong evidence that particle release is mechanically linked to cell movement.

result: Particles released by macrophages are enriched in focal adhesion proteins and cytoskeletal components. Proteomic analysis identified 653 proteins in particle preparations and 715 in plasma membrane preparations, with 502 in common. The top 15 focal adhesion proteins were more abundant in particle preparations.
evaluation: Claims C3, C30-C32, and C88 are supported by shotgun proteomics data (Figure 5) from three independent preparations. The enrichment of focal adhesion proteins in particles is consistent with the proposed mechanism of particle release during filopodia/lamellipodia movement. However, the claim that proteins are "relatively more abundant" (C32) requires clarification on whether this is statistically significant across all 15 proteins.

result: Inhibiting focal adhesion disassembly with an FAK inhibitor increases particle release. FAK inhibitor-treated macrophages retained mobile filopodia/lamellipodia but released lawns of particles approximately twice the size of the cell body, compared to ~40% in DMSO-treated controls.
evaluation: Claims C33-C38 and C40 are supported by live-cell imaging and SEM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The quantification (C36) is based on 10 macrophages per group, which is a relatively small sample size. However, the authors acknowledge the difficulty in accurately quantifying particle numbers. The finding is consistent with the proposed mechanism that interfering with focal adhesion disassembly increases particle release.

result: Particles released by macrophages are enriched in accessible cholesterol (detectable with ALO-D4) but not in sphingolipid-sequestered cholesterol (detectable with OlyA). NanoSIMS imaging showed ~twofold higher 15N enrichment from [15N]ALO-D4 in particles compared to the cell body, while 13C enrichment from [13C]OlyA was very low.
evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C24, C25, C39, C41, C42, C44, C45, C63, and C89 are well-supported by multiple complementary techniques including STED microscopy (Figure 6) and NanoSIMS imaging (Figures 3, 7, 8). The quantification shows statistically significant enrichment (p<0.001) of accessible cholesterol in particles. The sphingomyelinase control experiments (C43) validate the specificity of OlyA binding.

result: The plasma membrane shows distinct spatial distributions of accessible and sphingolipid-sequestered cholesterol. A fine linear band of 15N enrichment (accessible cholesterol) at the extreme outer edge of cells extends beyond a broad band of 13C enrichment (sphingolipid-sequestered cholesterol) corresponding to actin-rich lamellipodia.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 and C67-C71 are supported by high-resolution NanoSIMS imaging (Figures 7, 8) showing distinct spatial patterns of ALO-D4 and OlyA binding. The correlation with phalloidin staining (C49) confirms that OlyA binding corresponds to actin-rich lamellipodia. The interpretation that accessible cholesterol is enriched at the far edge (C70) is a reasonable inference from the data, though C71 is more speculative.

result: Particles contain plasma membrane proteins as demonstrated by biotinylation experiments. Biotinylated cell-surface proteins in particles were detectable with fluorescent streptavidin and streptavidin-conjugated gold nanoparticles by both fluorescence microscopy and SEM.
evaluation: Claims C26-C29 are supported by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 4A) and SEM with immunogold labeling (Figure 4B). The negative control (C28) showing no binding to non-biotinylated cells validates the specificity. NanoSIMS detection of 14N and 32S (C29) provides additional evidence for protein content in particles.

result: Blocking particle release with blebbistatin increases [3H]cholesterol retention in macrophages and decreases [3H]cholesterol in the particle fraction. Conversely, LXR agonist treatment reduces cellular [3H]cholesterol and increases [3H]cholesterol in particles.
evaluation: Claims C52, C53, and C81 are supported by scintillation counting data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) showing statistically significant differences (p<0.001 or p<0.01). The experiments were performed in the absence of cholesterol acceptors, demonstrating that particle release contributes to cholesterol efflux. However, the number of independent experiments is not clearly stated.

result: HDL markedly increases efflux of [3H]cholesterol from cholesterol-loaded macrophages into the cell culture medium.
evaluation: Claim C54 is supported by scintillation counting data (Figure 8—figure supplement 2) showing statistically significant increase (p<0.001) in [3H]cholesterol efflux with HDL treatment. This serves as a positive control demonstrating that the established HDL-mediated cholesterol efflux pathway is functional in this system.

result: Macrophages release biotinylated particles onto collagen IV matrix that are enriched in accessible cholesterol. The collagen beneath the lawn of particles was depleted, likely reflecting digestion by filopodia/lamellipodia.
evaluation: Claims C55 and C56 are well-supported by SEM (Figure 9A) and STED microscopy (Figure 9B) showing particle release onto collagen matrix with colocalization of ALO-D4 and streptavidin binding. However, C57 is an interpretation without direct evidence of collagen digestion (no protease activity assays or time-course studies). The collagen depletion could have alternative explanations.

result: Macrophages release particles onto dead cells and adjacent endothelial cells. Live-cell microscopy showed a live macrophage extending lamellipodia over a dead macrophage, and SEM revealed particle release onto both the substrate and the dead cell surface. Biotinylated particles were also detected on adjacent endothelial cells.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by live-cell imaging (Figure 10—video 1) and SEM (Figure 10, Figure 10—figure supplement 1). However, C61 is an inference based on the distribution pattern of gold nanoparticles on endothelial cells. The authors acknowledge they could not definitively identify individual particles on endothelial cells due to complex membrane topography, making this interpretation uncertain.

result: Sphingomyelinase treatment markedly reduces or abolishes OlyA and lysenin binding to macrophages and CHO cells.
evaluation: Claim C43 is supported by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) showing loss of OlyA and lysenin binding after sphingomyelinase treatment. This control validates that OlyA and lysenin specifically bind sphingomyelin-associated cholesterol and sphingomyelin, respectively.

result: FAK inhibitor treatment does not change the patterns of ALO-D4 and OlyA binding to particles or the macrophage cell body.
evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by NanoSIMS images (Figure 7—figure supplements 4-6) showing similar patterns of accessible and sphingolipid-sequestered cholesterol distribution in FAK inhibitor-treated cells compared to controls. This indicates that FAK inhibition increases particle quantity but not cholesterol composition.

result: According to the Raghupathy model, sphingolipid-associated cholesterol on the outer leaflet associates indirectly with the actin cytoskeleton and would remain tethered during filopodia/lamellipodia movement, while mobile accessible cholesterol would be more likely to be left behind on the substrate.
evaluation: Claims C64-C66 describe a model from prior literature (Raghupathy et al., 2015) and inferences based on that model. While the authors' data (C67-C71) are consistent with this model, these claims represent a mechanistic hypothesis rather than directly demonstrated findings. The model provides a plausible explanation but has not been directly tested in this study.

result: Background and context from prior literature on cholesterol efflux mechanisms, previous observations of particle release from macrophages and other cells, and comparison with related phenomena like migrasomes.
evaluation: Claims C8-C16 and C72-C79, C82 accurately represent established knowledge and prior work from the literature, supported by appropriate citations. These provide context for the current study. The comparisons with prior work (C72-C79) appropriately distinguish the current findings from related phenomena.

result: Macrophages can release plasma membrane-derived particles onto physiologic substrates (collagen matrix, dead cells), lending plausibility to the notion that particle release could occur in vivo.
evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by experiments showing particle release on collagen (C55-C56) and dead cells (C58-C59). However, the inference that this "lends plausibility" to in vivo occurrence is speculative. The in vitro conditions may not fully recapitulate the in vivo environment, and direct evidence of particle release in living tissues is not provided.

result: Particle release could facilitate the return of accessible cholesterol into circulation and could contribute to extracellular cholesterol deposition in atherosclerotic plaques. The discovery is likely relevant to cholesterol efflux and could have implications for atherosclerosis.
evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are speculative statements about potential physiological and pathological relevance. While the data show that particle release contributes to cholesterol efflux in vitro (C52, C81), the claims about in vivo relevance to reverse cholesterol transport (C83) and atherosclerosis (C84, C86) are not directly tested. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future investigation but are not supported by the current data.

result: Focal adhesions are macromolecular assemblies that link the actin cytoskeleton inside cells to the extracellular substrate.
evaluation: Claim C87 is established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. This provides necessary background for understanding the role of focal adhesion proteins in particle release.
